title: Titus Brandsma (1881–1942)
hookLine: a Dutch Carmelite who carried a letter from editor to editor, telling Catholic papers to refuse Nazi propaganda

cards: A train compartment in the occupied Netherlands. A small, thin priest in a Carmelite habit, glasses, a briefcase on his knees. Inside the briefcase is a letter from the Dutch bishops.
He gets off in one town, finds the office of the local Catholic newspaper, sits down with the editor, and explains the letter. Then back to the station, and the next town, and the next editor.
He knows the occupiers will hear about this. Titus Brandsma, friar, professor and newspaperman, keeps going anyway.

teach.b: First, the professor. Titus was a Carmelite friar and a scholar of mysticism, a teacher at the Catholic university in Nijmegen. He also loved newspapers.
He wrote for them, edited, and served as spiritual adviser to the Catholic journalists of his country. Second, the order.

teach.h: NO NAZI PROPAGANDA IN OUR PAPERS.
teach.b: Under the occupation, the Nazi authorities demanded that Catholic papers print their propaganda, including notices for the Dutch Nazi party.

The bishops said no: a Catholic paper that printed it could no longer call itself Catholic. Somebody had to carry that message to the editors, face to face, so no one could say they hadn't heard. Titus said he would go.
Third, the cost. He was arrested and questioned. Asked why he resisted, he said, in substance, that the Nazi ideas could not be squared with the Gospel.
He was sent from prison to prison, then to Dachau. Weak and sick, he was taken to the camp hospital and killed with an injection. Tradition says he gave his rosary to the nurse who did it.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.
teach.b: Jesus says in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
Set beside his life, it reads like a rule for newsrooms too: telling the truth includes refusing to print a lie, even a paid one.

how: Catholics honor St. Titus Brandsma as a martyr, and Catholic journalists' groups name him as a patron and example; Carmelites keep his feast.

practice: Think of a place where you speak to more than one person: a team chat, a family thread, a meeting. Is there something true that needs saying there, plainly and kindly, or something false you've let pass?
Choose one sentence and say it to yourself slowly until it's clear and fair; if you pray, ask for Titus's steadiness.
